Negative Binomial and Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Regression by IRLS and EM

STA 651 Final Project: the nbzinbHossen R package

Arman Hossen

2026-11-01

Source: vignettes/articles/report.qmd

1 Introduction

Many data in health research are counts: the number of hospital visits in a month, or the number of research papers published. Poisson regression is useful in that case, but it has a very strong assumption: the mean and the variance must be equal. This is rarely true in a real data set. Most count data are overdispersed, with a variance greater than the mean, and many data sets also contain more zeros than a Poisson distribution allows.

The negative binomial (NB2) model handles overdispersion with a dispersion parameter θ\theta, so that Var(Y)=μ+μ2/θ\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta. When the extra zeros come from a different process, for example a person who never sees a doctor, a zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model fits more naturally. It treats each observation either as a structural zero or as a draw from an NB distribution, which can itself be zero.

In this project, I built the R package nbzinbHossen, which fits both models:

  • NB regression by iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS), alternated with Newton–Raphson updates of log⁡θ\log\theta;
  • ZINB regression by an EM algorithm whose M-steps are IRLS fits.

I did not use any general-purpose optimizer such as optim(), or glm() fitting code. I check the package against MASS::glm.nb() and pscl::zeroinfl() on two data sets, test by simulation whether zinbreg() recovers known parameters, and use it to analyse the NMES1988 data.

2 Methods

2.1 Negative binomial (NB2) regression

For counts YiY_i with covariates xix_i, offset oio_i and prior weights aia_i, P(Yi=y)=Γ(y+θ)Γ(θ)y!(θθ+μi)θ(μiθ+μi)y,log⁡μi=ηi=xi⊤β+oi, P(Y_i = y) = \frac{\Gamma(y+\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)\,y!} \Big(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\mu_i}\Big)^{\theta} \Big(\frac{\mu_i}{\theta+\mu_i}\Big)^{y}, \qquad \log\mu_i = \eta_i = x_i^\top\beta + o_i, so E(Yi)=μiE(Y_i)=\mu_i and Var(Yi)=μi+μi2/θ\mathrm{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i+\mu_i^2/\theta. The log-likelihood is ℓ(β,θ)=∑iai[log⁡Γ(yi+θ)−log⁡Γ(θ)−log⁡yi!+θlog⁡θ+yilog⁡μi−(θ+yi)log⁡(θ+μi)]. \ell(\beta,\theta)=\sum_i a_i\big[\log\Gamma(y_i+\theta)-\log\Gamma(\theta) -\log y_i!+\theta\log\theta+y_i\log\mu_i-(\theta+y_i)\log(\theta+\mu_i)\big].

IRLS for β\beta (θ\theta fixed). With the log link, (∂μ/∂η)2=μ2(\partial\mu/\partial\eta)^2=\mu^2, so Fisher scoring is weighted least squares with wi=aiθμiθ+μi,zi=(ηi−oi)+yi−μiμi,β(t+1)=(X⊤WX)−1X⊤Wz. w_i = a_i\frac{\theta\mu_i}{\theta+\mu_i},\qquad z_i = (\eta_i-o_i) + \frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\mu_i},\qquad \beta^{(t+1)} = (X^\top W X)^{-1}X^\top W z . The solve uses the QR decomposition of W1/2XW^{1/2}X. Because the log link is not canonical for the NB, a Fisher-scoring step is not guaranteed to increase ℓ\ell, so the step is halved whenever ℓ\ell would decrease.

Newton–Raphson for θ\theta (β\beta fixed). With ψ\psi and ψ′\psi' the digamma and trigamma functions, U(θ)=∑iai[ψ(yi+θ)−ψ(θ)+log⁡θ+1−log⁡(θ+μi)−yi+θθ+μi], U(\theta)=\sum_i a_i\Big[\psi(y_i+\theta)-\psi(\theta)+\log\theta+1-\log(\theta+\mu_i)-\frac{y_i+\theta}{\theta+\mu_i}\Big], H(θ)=∑iai[ψ′(yi+θ)−ψ′(θ)+1θ−2θ+μi+yi+θ(θ+μi)2]. H(\theta)=\sum_i a_i\Big[\psi'(y_i+\theta)-\psi'(\theta)+\frac1\theta-\frac{2}{\theta+\mu_i}+\frac{y_i+\theta}{(\theta+\mu_i)^2}\Big]. We update ϕ=log⁡θ\phi=\log\theta, which keeps θ>0\theta>0: Uϕ=θUU_\phi=\theta U, Hϕ=θ2H+θUH_\phi=\theta^2H+\theta U, ϕ←ϕ−Uϕ/Hϕ\phi\leftarrow\phi-U_\phi/H_\phi. If Hϕ≥0H_\phi\ge 0 a unit step in the direction of UϕU_\phi is taken, and steps are halved until ℓ\ell does not decrease.

Outer loop. Start from a Poisson IRLS fit and the moment estimate θ0=∑iai/∑iai(yi/μi−1)2\theta_0=\sum_i a_i/\sum_i a_i(y_i/\mu_i-1)^2. Then alternate the two updates until |ℓ(t+1)−ℓ(t)|<10−8|\ell^{(t+1)}-\ell^{(t)}|<10^{-8}. If θ\theta reaches a large cap (10610^6) the data show no overdispersion and a warning is given.

Standard errors. As in glm.nb(), Var̂(β̂)=(X⊤ŴX)−1\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)=(X^\top\hat WX)^{-1} treating θ\theta as known, and SE(θ̂)={−H(θ̂)}−1/2\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta)=\{-H(\hat\theta)\}^{-1/2}.

2.2 Zero-inflated negative binomial regression

With probability πi\pi_i observation ii is a structural zero, otherwise it is NB(μi,θ)(\mu_i,\theta): P(Yi=0)=πi+(1−πi)f0(μi,θ),P(Yi=y)=(1−πi)fNB(y;μi,θ),y≥1, P(Y_i=0)=\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)f_0(\mu_i,\theta),\quad P(Y_i=y)=(1-\pi_i)f_{NB}(y;\mu_i,\theta),\ y\ge1, where f0={θ/(θ+μi)}θf_0=\{\theta/(\theta+\mu_i)\}^\theta, log⁡μi=xi⊤β+oi\log\mu_i=x_i^\top\beta+o_i and logitπi=zi⊤γ\mathrm{logit}\,\pi_i=z_i^\top\gamma. The observed-data log-likelihood ℓ(β,γ,θ)=∑yi=0log⁡[πi+(1−πi)f0]+∑yi>0[log⁡(1−πi)+log⁡fNB(yi;μi,θ)] \ell(\beta,\gamma,\theta)=\sum_{y_i=0}\log\big[\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)f_0\big] +\sum_{y_i>0}\big[\log(1-\pi_i)+\log f_{NB}(y_i;\mu_i,\theta)\big] contains the log of a sum, so it is not an exponential-family GLM likelihood and cannot be maximized by IRLS directly. We use the EM algorithm with latent indicators Di=1D_i=1 for structural zeros.

E-step. τi=P(Di=1∣yi)=πi/{πi+(1−πi)f0}\tau_i=P(D_i=1\mid y_i)=\pi_i/\{\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)f_0\} if yi=0y_i=0, and τi=0\tau_i=0 if yi>0y_i>0.

M-step, zero part. Maximize ∑i[τilog⁡πi+(1−τi)log⁡(1−πi)]\sum_i[\tau_i\log\pi_i+(1-\tau_i)\log(1-\pi_i)]: a logistic regression with fractional response τi\tau_i, fitted by IRLS with wi=πi(1−πi)w_i=\pi_i(1-\pi_i) and zi=zi⊤γ+(τi−πi)/{πi(1−πi)}z_i=z_i^\top\gamma+(\tau_i-\pi_i)/\{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\}.

M-step, count part. Maximize ∑i(1−τi)log⁡fNB(yi;μi,θ)\sum_i(1-\tau_i)\log f_{NB}(y_i;\mu_i,\theta): exactly the NB fit above with prior weights ai=1−τia_i=1-\tau_i, warm-started at the current (β,θ)(\beta,\theta).

Starting values and convergence. (β,θ)(\beta,\theta) come from the NB fit and γ\gamma from an IRLS logistic regression of I(yi=0)I(y_i=0) on ziz_i. EM stops when ℓ\ell changes by less than 10−1010^{-10}. The package records ℓ\ell at every iteration and warns if it ever decreases. This never happened in any fit reported here.

Standard errors (analytic Hessian). EM gives no standard errors, so we invert the observed information of ℓ\ell in (β,γ,log⁡θ)(\beta,\gamma,\log\theta). Each ℓi\ell_i depends on β\beta only through ηi\eta_i and on γ\gamma only through ζi=zi⊤γ\zeta_i=z_i^\top\gamma. The Hessian is therefore built from per-observation second derivatives, e.g. Hββ=X⊤diag(ai∂2ℓi/∂ηi2)XH_{\beta\beta}=X^\top\mathrm{diag}(a_i\,\partial^2\ell_i/\partial\eta_i^2)X. For yi>0y_i>0 these are NB and logistic derivatives, e.g. ∂2ℓi/∂ηi2=−θμi(θ+yi)/(θ+μi)2\partial^2\ell_i/\partial\eta_i^2=-\theta\mu_i(\theta+y_i)/(\theta+\mu_i)^2. For yi=0y_i=0, write ℓi=log⁡Li\ell_i=\log L_i with Li=πi+(1−πi)egiL_i=\pi_i+(1-\pi_i)e^{g_i} and gi=θlog⁡{θ/(θ+μi)}g_i=\theta\log\{\theta/(\theta+\mu_i)\}. With ri=(1−πi)egi/Li=1−τir_i=(1-\pi_i)e^{g_i}/L_i=1-\tau_i and ∂ri/∂gi=ri(1−ri)\partial r_i/\partial g_i=r_i(1-r_i), ∂2ℓi∂u∂v=rigi,uv+ri(1−ri)gi,ugi,v,u,v∈{ηi,log⁡θ}, \frac{\partial^2\ell_i}{\partial u\,\partial v}=r_i\,g_{i,uv}+r_i(1-r_i)\,g_{i,u}\,g_{i,v}, \qquad u,v\in\{\eta_i,\log\theta\}, and the cross terms with ζi\zeta_i are −πi(1−πi)egigi,u/Li2-\pi_i(1-\pi_i)e^{g_i}g_{i,u}/L_i^2. All terms are listed in R/zinb_hessian.R. The analytic Hessian agrees with numDeriv::hessian() to about 10−710^{-7} relative error (checked in the tests). We report log⁡θ\log\theta with its SE, as zeroinfl() does, and SE(θ̂)=θ̂SE(log⁡θ̂)\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta)=\hat\theta\,\mathrm{SE}(\log\hat\theta) by the delta method.

3 The R package

The package nbzinbHossen is installed with

devtools::install_github("armanhossen-am/nbzinbHossen")
Function Purpose
nbreg(formula, data, subset, na.action, weights, offset, control) NB regression by IRLS + Newton–Raphson for log⁡θ\log\theta
zinbreg(formula, data, subset, na.action, weights, offset, control) ZINB regression by EM with IRLS M-steps; formula y ~ count | zero
nbreg_control(), zinbreg_control() tolerances, iteration limits, trace, Hessian type

Both functions return S3 objects ("nbreg", "zinbreg") holding the coefficients, covariance matrix, θ̂\hat\theta and its SE, log-likelihood, number of iterations, a convergence flag, fitted values and the call. Methods: print, summary (+ print.summary), coef, vcov, logLik (with a df attribute, so AIC()/BIC() work), fitted, residuals (response, Pearson; deviance for NB), nobs and predict with newdata (type = "response", "count", "zero" and "prob" for ZINB). The numerical work is in R/utils.R (weighted least squares, IRLS and Newton–Raphson loops), R/nbreg.R, R/zinbreg.R and R/zinb_hessian.R; none of it calls optim(), glm(), lm() or any other fitting routine. Tests in tests/testthat/ compare both functions with the reference implementations and check offsets, weights, single-covariate models, EM monotonicity, error messages and warnings. devtools::check() gives 0 errors, 0 warnings and 0 notes, and the GitHub Actions workflow runs it on macOS, Windows and Linux.

A short example:

fit <- zinbreg(art ~ fem + kid5 + ment | ment, data = bioChemists)
round(coef(fit), 3)
count_(Intercept)    count_femWomen        count_kid5        count_ment
            0.494            -0.228            -0.131             0.024
 zero_(Intercept)         zero_ment
           -0.795            -0.619 
fit$theta
[1] 2.695733
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(fem = "Women", kid5 = 0, ment = c(0, 20)),
        type = "zero")
           1            2
3.111162e-01 1.883220e-06

4 Benchmarking

We compare our fits with glm.nb() (with epsilon = 1e-10) and zeroinfl() (with reltol = 1e-12) on pscl::bioChemists (n = 915) and AER::NMES1988 (n = 4406), using the full models of Section 5 of the project description. Table 1 summarizes the maximum absolute differences. Every one is far inside the required tolerance. The side-by-side estimates are in the appendix (Table 8 to Table 11).

nbreg() is about as fast as glm.nb(). zinbreg() is several times slower than zeroinfl() because EM converges linearly: it needed 135 iterations on bioChemists and 66 on NMES1988, each with a full IRLS fit in both M-steps. Every fit still takes under a second.

Figure 1 shows that the log-likelihood never decreases, as EM guarantees. Almost all of the gain comes in the first few iterations. After that, the distance to the optimum shrinks by a roughly constant factor per iteration, a straight line on the log scale: the linear convergence typical of EM.

5 Simulation study

We simulated R=200R = 200 data sets of size n=500n = 500 from a ZINB model with log⁡μi=1+0.5x1i−0.4x2i\log\mu_i = 1 + 0.5x_{1i} - 0.4x_{2i}, where x1∼N(0,1)x_1\sim N(0,1) and x2∼Bernoulli(0.5)x_2\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.5). The zero part is logitπi=−1+0.8wi\mathrm{logit}\,\pi_i = -1 + 0.8w_i with w∼N(0,1)w\sim N(0,1), and θ=1.5\theta = 1.5. Each data set was fitted with zinbreg(y ~ x1 + x2 | w) (seed 651). 200 of 200 fits converged, with a median of 88 EM iterations. Table 3 reports the bias, the mean estimated SE against the Monte Carlo SD of the estimates, and the coverage of 95% Wald intervals. With 200 replications the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage near 0.95 is about 0.015.

The estimates are close to unbiased. The largest bias, −0.065-0.065 for the zero-part intercept, is less than a fifth of that estimate’s Monte Carlo SD, and the count-part slopes are essentially unbiased.

The average estimated SEs track the Monte Carlo SDs but are slightly smaller for most parameters, most visibly for the binary covariate x2x_2 (0.121 against 0.141). Coverage of the 95% Wald intervals runs from 0.905 to 0.945. With a Monte Carlo SE of about 0.015, the intervals for x2x_2 (0.905) and log⁡θ\log\theta (0.915) under-cover slightly.

Both shortfalls are plausible at n=500n = 500. A binary covariate carries less information than a continuous one, and θ\theta is partly confounded with the zero-inflation probability, since both change how many zeros appear. The zero-part intercept is the least precisely estimated parameter (MC SD 0.36), because only the zeros carry information about π\pi.

6 Data analysis: NMES1988

The data have n=4406n = 4406 individuals aged 66 and over. The response is visits, the number of physician office visits. The count part uses hospital, health, chronic, gender, school and insurance; the zero part uses hospital, chronic, gender, school and insurance.

6.1 Descriptive summary

Visits are strongly overdispersed: the variance (45.7) is almost eight times the mean (5.77). There are also far more zeros than a Poisson model allows. 683 people (15.5%) made no visits, while a Poisson distribution with the same mean puts only 0.3% of its mass at zero, about 14 people. Figure 2 shows the Poisson missing both the spike at zero and the long right tail, which reaches 89 visits.

6.2 Model comparison

The observed number of zeros is 683. The NB model estimates θ̂=1.207\hat\theta = 1.207 (SE 0.034) and the ZINB model θ̂=1.483\hat\theta = 1.483 (SE 0.052).

The Poisson model fits very poorly: its AIC is about 11,600 higher than NB’s, and it predicts 47 zeros against 683. Allowing overdispersion closes most of that gap. Unlike in the bioChemists example, though, the NB model still under-predicts the zeros (608 against 683).

The ZINB model predicts 709 zeros, slightly too many but closer than NB. Both criteria favour ZINB: its AIC is 148 lower and its BIC 109 lower, even though BIC penalises its six extra parameters heavily. The log-likelihood improves by 79.9.

A formal likelihood-ratio test is awkward because NB lies on the boundary of the ZINB parameter space (π→0\pi \to 0), but an improvement this large is far beyond what six extra parameters produce by chance. The dispersion estimate rises from 1.21 (NB) to 1.48 (ZINB), because the zero process now explains part of the extra variation.

6.3 Interpretation

The number of doctor visits varies widely. The NB model allows more variation than the Poisson model. At a mean of 5.77 visits, the estimated NB variance is about 33.

In the ZINB count part, we compare people while keeping the other factors the same:

  • Each extra hospital stay is linked to 22% more expected visits.
  • Poor health is linked to 33% more visits than average health.
  • Excellent health is linked to 27% fewer visits than average health.
  • Each extra chronic condition is linked to 14% more visits.
  • Men have 8% fewer expected visits than women.
  • Each extra year of schooling is linked to 2% more visits.
  • Private insurance is linked to 13% more visits.

All these relationships are statistically significant at the 5% level.

The zero part describes the odds of being in the model’s non-user group. Each extra chronic condition lowers these odds by 71%. Private insurance lowers them by 69%. Each extra year of schooling lowers them by 8%. Men have almost twice the odds of women. Hospital stays are linked to lower odds, but this result is not statistically significant.

Both models show similar patterns. Some differences are smaller in the ZINB count part. For example, insurance is linked to 25% more visits in NB but 13% more in ZINB. ZINB also shows that insured people are less likely to belong to the non-user group. People outside this group can still have zero visits.

6.4 Which model?

I prefer the ZINB model for these data. It has the lowest AIC and BIC of the three, it reproduces the number of zeros better than NB, and its two parts tell a sensible story about health-care use in old age. One process decides whether a person sees a physician at all, and it depends strongly on chronic illness, insurance, gender and education. A second process decides how often users visit, and it depends mainly on health status and hospital stays. The cost is six extra parameters and a slight over-prediction of zeros (709 against 683). A hurdle model, which puts all zeros in one process, would be a reasonable alternative to compare against.

7 Discussion

The package reproduces glm.nb() and zeroinfl() closely without a general-purpose optimizer, but the approach has limits.

  • Speed. EM converges only linearly (Figure 1): zinbreg() needed 66 iterations on NMES1988 and 135 on bioChemists, and ran about 5 to 9 times slower than zeroinfl(). SQUAREM acceleration, or switching to Newton’s method on the observed-data likelihood once EM is near the optimum, would cut this.
  • NB standard errors. Like glm.nb(), nbreg() treats θ\theta as known when computing SE(β̂)\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta), so those SEs ignore the uncertainty in θ̂\hat\theta.
  • Interval coverage. The simulation showed Wald intervals under-covering slightly at n=500n = 500 (0.905 for the binary covariate). Profile-likelihood or bootstrap intervals would be more reliable.
  • Local maxima. EM can in principle stop at a local maximum, so results depend on starting values. Ours (an NB fit plus a logistic regression of the zero indicator) reached the same optimum as zeroinfl() in every case tried, but that is not guaranteed.
  • Offsets. Offsets are supported only in the count part.

Natural extensions are a zero-inflated Poisson option, hurdle models, robust (sandwich) standard errors, a probit or complementary log-log link for the zero part, and the Vuong test for comparing NB with ZINB.

8 AI-use statement

I used Claude Code throughout this project, as the assignment intended. Claude Code set up the package structure and CLAUDE.md, and wrote the fitting code (IRLS for the NB coefficients, Newton–Raphson for log⁡θ\log\theta, the EM algorithm and the analytic Hessian), the S3 methods, the tests, the benchmark and simulation scripts, the GitHub Actions workflow and the pkgdown configuration. It also drafted the other sections of this report and all of its code. I wrote the interpretation of the NMES1988 results (the Interpretation subsection) myself, rewrote the introduction in my own words, and edited the other sections.

What I verified myself: I tested the package myself in R. I installed it from GitHub with devtools::install_github("armanhossen-am/nbzinbHossen"), and it installed without errors. I then ran the models myself, including the zinbreg() example on the bioChemists data, and everything ran correctly: the summary showed the count and zero-inflation coefficient tables, theta and the log-likelihood, and predict() returned the structural-zero probabilities.

One improvement I directed: I asked Claude Code to add a figure showing the EM log-likelihood climbing at every iteration. I had it add this to the package as a plot() method for zinbreg fits, with a test and documentation, and commit both changes to GitHub.
